If the mission forces or supporting echelons encounter any difficulties or if the situation changes, the mission planning cell is alerted immediately and the MEU and ARG commanders are notified if any significant alterations to the COA arise. If changes in the situation threaten the suitability of the COA and if time permits, the commanders may direct the staff and the mission planning cell to return to an earlier step in the planning process.

The mission commander immediately passes the results of COA comparison and decision to the forces to assist their planning and preparations. The mission commander and the mission planning cell continue to update and forward planning details as changes occur. Plans for supporting or contingency missions may also be developed. Such missions may be mass casualty, medical evacuation, platoon-size reinforcement, initial terminal guidance, linkup, evasion, or recovery. Supporting echelons, such as ships or other MSEs, receive updated information from their liaison officers inside the mission planning cell. The mission planning cell produces a confirmation brief, which serves as the draft OPORD.

The MEU S-3 creates and delivers the graphic and written CONOPS in addition to other documents required by HHQ. To save time and ensure coordinated execution, the commander may not approve the completed final order until after the confirmation brief.

The commander approves the mission for execution immediately following the confirmation brief; therefore, the confirmation brief is the primary tool used to transition from planning to execution. It is also the optimum means of final coordination within the time available and it can serve as a form of rehearsal. The brief’s purpose is to ensure those involved in executing the plan completely understand it and achieve situational awareness.

The brief also ensures agreement among force elements, since all critical participants are present. Because the confirmation brief is primarily for those who have a role in executing the mission, all available members of the mission planning cell and the mission force should attend. Supporting elements, such as ship personnel, not represented in the mission planning cell should also attend. All standby and follow-on mission planning cells that might be affected by the primary mission should also observe the brief. The CAT and battlestaff members should attend to provide expertise and answer questions.

Using the format in the unit planning SOP, the confirmation brief is conducted by the mission commander. Each participant uses the SOP’s format and media in the brief to avoid overlaps or omissions. The presentation media are collected by the scribe and assembled into a smart pack that may serve as the written order. An initial version of the smart pack may be assembled during orders development, but it should not be issued until sanctioned by the commander at the confirmation brief. The original confirmation brief’s contents, together with any resulting changes or decisions, must be provided to the R&S force, particularly if no representative attended, to ensure that the final, approved mission is understood.

The brief’s major focus is on actions occurring in the objective area. The commander of the element executing these actions, such as the raid force commander, provides a detailed explanation of the intended actions and the specific tasks assigned to subordinate elements. During the brief, the commanders and their staffs identify any potential problems. Conflicts that arise from the brief are resolved or planned for prior to the completion of the brief. Additional planning must occur if anything is briefed that is not yet planned for or coordinated.

The primary mission confirmation brief is usually limited to an hour. The MEU and ARG commanders may schedule confirmation briefs for standby or follow-on missions following completion of the primary mission brief. Upon completion of the primary mission brief, various elements of the force may conduct supporting briefs to the same audience. The commander then designates time for subordinate element leaders to accomplish any remaining preparations and rehearsals and a final inspection of troops and equipment is conducted to ensure mission readiness.

During the period before the launch of forces, the MEU and ARG command echelons supervise the final preparations and coordination of subordinate elements and prepare for their own role in the command and control of the operation. The SOPs establish command and control procedures for various types of operations except that preparation time is limited. Assumptions and preconditions are validated and branch and sequel planning should occur.

Table H-1 is a sample planning matrix. Units normally develop their own timelines and SOPs. (The sample matrix lays out a notional 0:00-6:00 R2P2 timeline across problem framing, COA development, COA war game/comparison and decision, orders development, and transition, cross-referencing who acts (CAT, battlestaff, amphibious task force), the command and staff actions, the products generated at each step, and concurrent/parallel actions such as R&S planning and command and staff supervision.)

chapters.chapter_overview: This appendix addresses how joint and multinational operations are coordinated with US Government departments and agencies, international organizations, NGOs, host nation agencies, and the private sector, and how that coordination is reflected in Annex V of the OPORD/OPLAN.

paragraphs.details: Joint and multinational operations are integrated at the strategic level and coordinated at the operational and tactical level with the activities of participating US Government departments and agencies, relevant international organizations, NGOs, host nation agencies, and elements of the private sector to achieve common objectives. Refer to JP 3-08, Interorganizational Cooperation, for additional information.

Annex V (Interagency/Interorganizational Coordination) of the OPORD or OPLAN reflects the commander’s priorities and approach to interorganizational cooperation. Information in the annex provides a basis for staff and liaison interaction with these numerous organizations and agencies. Continued coordination strengthens the whole of government efforts and improves the probability of mission success. In developing Annex V, consideration should be given to—
• Key Interagency Strategies. Marine Corps planners must become familiar with interagency strategies, assessments, and plans at all levels (see table I-1). Requests for relevant interagency strategies, such as counternarcotics or counterterrorism, must be made through the appropriate interagency coordination center within each geographic combatant command or Marine Corps component command. A basic understanding of these strategies, assessments, or plans is critical to enable interagency activities.
• Assessment and Planning Frameworks. Interagency partners in many cases have developed assessment tools and have conducted or are conducting assessments in the area of operations. These assessments, coupled with their authorities, make interagency coordination a valuable process. This is especially true for operations in the information environment, where the application of military information power complements diplomatic efforts, federal law enforcement agencies as well as cyberspace and space operations. All security cooperation events will require assessment, monitoring, and evaluation to determine the outcomes of partner capability development. (For more information, see JP 3-20, Security Cooperation.) Assessment tools, such as the Interagency Conflict Assessment Framework, should be the starting point for an interagency team to assess conflict systematically and collaboratively prepare for interagency planning. Planners may employ other tools, such as Measuring Peace in Conflict Environments (MPICE): A Metrics Framework and the Interagency Management System for Reconstruction and Stabilization, to facilitate interagency activities. The United States Institute of Peace publication Guiding Principles for Stabilization and Reconstruction is an example of a reference that would augment the applicable joint doctrine, such as JP 3-07, Stability. A liaison or staff officer assigned to interorganizational cooperation needs to study the relevant joint and agency publications. Interagency planning structures will not supersede Marine Corps planning structures.

Table I-1 lists key interagency documents Marine Corps planners should be familiar with: the Department of Defense’s Guidance for Employment of the Force (an annual classified document prioritizing theater strategic end states, including interagency cooperation and integration); USAID’s Country Development Cooperation Strategy (a five-year look at a country’s needs); Department of State bureaus’ Bureau Strategic Plan (annual interagency objectives and performance result indicators); the Integrated Country Strategy (ICS), produced by the chief of mission and all other US Government agencies on the country team (annual interagency objectives by priority); and the USAID mission-in-country Operational Plan (an annual plan feeding into the mission support plan).

chapters.chapter_name: Appendix J - Basic Operation Plan, Operation Order, and Attachments
chapters.chapter_overview: Appendix J provides the instructions and formats, based on CJCSM 3130.03B, that govern development of a Marine Corps basic operation plan (OPLAN) or operation order (OPORD); Section I gives the general administrative guidance for paragraph numbering, classification marking, page numbering, and a line-by-line explanation of the basic order's content, while Section II provides sample formats for a plan summary, the basic order/plan, and a representative subset of Marine Corps-specific annexes, appendices, tabs, and exhibits, plus a CJCSM joint-format example table of contents.
chapters.schema_note: The 'Joint Orders Table of Contents' (Section II, added by Change 1, based on CJCSM 3130.03B, 14 June 2024) uses a different annex taxonomy than the Marine Corps-specific sample annex list given earlier in this appendix and in the basic order sample. Independently verified divergences between the Marine Corps-specific listing (Appendix J pp. J-10 through J-14 and the basic order sample's ANNEXES block) and the joint/CJCSM listing (pp. J-70 through J-78): Annex D 'Logistics/Combat Service Support' vs. 'Logistics'; Annex I 'Information' vs. 'Knowledge, Information, and Data Management'; Annex K 'Combat Information Systems' vs. 'Command, Control, Communications, Computer, and Cybersecurity (C4/Cybersecurity) Systems'; Annex M 'Geospatial Information and Services' vs. '(Not Used)'; Annex N 'Space Operations' vs. 'Assessments'; Annex Q 'Medical Services' vs. 'Health Services'; Annex T 'Network Engagement' vs. 'Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Response'; Annex U 'Information Management' vs. 'Notional Counterproliferation Decision Guide'; Annex V 'Interagency/Interorganizational Coordination' vs. 'Interagency-Interorganizational Coordination'; Annex W 'Aviation Operations' vs. 'Operational Contract Support'; and Annexes F (Public Affairs), O (Foreign Disclosure Guidance), and Y (Commanders' Communication Strategy) appear only in the joint listing. A third, non-doctrinal variant appears as specimen text inside Figure J-3 (which lists F but omits I, R, and T, and titles D 'Logistics' and V 'Interagency Coordination') - illustrative dummy content, not a normative listing. These reflect two coexisting numbering conventions (Marine Corps-specific vs. joint/CJCSM) rather than an extraction error. No real internal paragraph-numbering scheme exists for this appendix itself, so synthetic sequential markers (J-¶n) were assigned in source order; the '1./a./(1)/(a)' numbering shown throughout is the OPORD format being taught (an eight-level cascade: 1. / a. / (1) / (a) / 1 / a / (1) / (a)), not this manual's own paragraph numbering. TREATMENT NOTE (revised by fidelity audit, 2026-09-09): Section I is a close, content-complete PARAPHRASE of the source, not a verbatim transcription - imperative source voice is rendered in the passive/declarative and sentences are condensed at roughly 70-85% of source length. It is faithful in substance and no line of the Line 1-41 walkthrough (both pages) is missing, but it should not be characterized as verbatim or zero-drift. Section II sample formats received purpose+structure catalog treatment rather than field-by-field transcription; every named sample-format heading in the source (16 sample formats plus the Joint Orders Table of Contents) has a corresponding subsection. Filled-in specimen text in Figures J-1/J-2/J-3 (dummy names such as I MEF, GREENTOWN/BLUELAND, M.B. TWINING, GENERAL C. THOMAS) was described rather than transcribed as illustrative example content; all instructive prose surrounding those figures is captured. SOURCE GAP (verified): the Line-by-Line walkthrough jumps from 'Line 15' to 'Lines 17-18' - no 'Line 16' entry exists in the source. OTHER SOURCE INCONSISTENCIES (verified, preserved): Annex D's narrative cites 'Appendix 1 (Supply)' although Appendix 1 is Petroleum, Oils, and Lubricants Supply and Appendix 7 is Supply; Annex B's own appendix list names Appendix 9 'Captured Enemy Equipment' while the Section II table of contents names it 'Captured Adversary Equipment'; and Tab A's Exhibit 3 is titled 'Operations' in Tab A's exhibit list but referenced as 'Exhibit I-6-A-3 (Information)' in Exhibit 2.

paragraphs.details: This appendix provides instructions and formats governing development of a basic operation plan and order (OPLAN/OPORD), based on CJCSM 3130.03B, Planning and Execution Formats and Guidance, for use by all staffs, subordinate commands, and support agencies. It applies to commanders of Marine Corps forces at all levels and contains two sections: Section I provides general administrative guidance for writing a basic operation plan or order (an operation plan/order foldout is included at the end of the publication for quick reference); Section II provides sample formats of a plan summary, operation plan or order, and other Marine Corps-specific attachments, plus a CJCSM-specific example joint order table of contents for use in a joint environment. Sample formats are descriptive, identifying the information to be placed in each paragraph, and are followed except when the commander's judgment requires modification; only those annexes, appendices, and tabs applicable to the level of command are required.

The arrangement of information in a basic operation plan or order conforms to the formats shown in this appendix. Paragraph and subparagraph headings indicated in the format always appear in each plan; in OPORDs, a paragraph not required is noted 'not applicable' to show it was considered. Further subdivisions conform to the paragraph titling/numbering system discussed below. The sequencing for naming supplemental documents to the basic plan/order is: annex, appendix, tab, exhibit. The last page of the basic plan/order and each attachment lists any included documents; the basic order/plan refers to each annex, and information in the basic order/plan is not normally repeated in the attachments.

Paragraph titles combine upper and lower case letters, underlined (e.g., Situation); subparagraphs and subtitles are likewise upper/lower case and underlined (e.g., Concept of Operations), except that forces, commands, or agencies are capitalized and underlined only in titles (e.g., SPECIAL PURPOSE MAGTF). A subdivided paragraph must have at least two subdivisions. When paragraphs are subdivided they are numbered and lettered in a cascading, progressively indented eight-level sequence: 1. then a. then (1) then (a) then 1 then a then (1) then (a), with the fifth through eighth levels shown underlined and without periods.

Subsequent lines of text for each paragraph may be aligned flush with the left margin or equally indented, as long as consistency is maintained throughout the document; the appendix shows both a flush-left and an equally-indented example of a sample paragraph 1a (Situation) entry.

Front and back covers are marked with the overall classification of the operation plan/order. The first page of each plan element (plan summary, basic plan, and each annex, appendix, tab, and exhibit) is marked with that element's overall classification; unclassified elements are marked as such. Each interior page of a classified element is marked with the highest classification and sensitive-information code word of material on that page, or marked unclassified if it contains no classified material. Classification markings are centered between the left and right margins at both the top and bottom of the page and written in uppercase letters (e.g., UNCLASSIFIED).

Every paragraph carries a security classification level, indicated by the parenthetical symbols (TS), (S), (C), and (U) placed before titles, paragraphs, and subparagraphs. For additional classification-marking guidance, see DoD Manual 5200.01 Volume 1, DoD Information Security Program: Overview, Classification, and Declassification.

Page numbers are located at the bottom of the page and centered. For example, page C-1-A-3 denotes page 3 of Tab A to Appendix 1 to Annex C. A single space separates the page number from the classification marking.
The formatting instructions give a line-by-line format for the OPLAN/OPORD. Line 1 is the Classification.

Line 2, Changes from Oral Orders, is used when oral orders regarding the operation were previously issued and is enclosed in parentheses (e.g., '(No change from oral orders except paragraphs 3b and 3f.)'); it is omitted in plans and in orders when no oral orders were issued.

Lines 3-7, Heading Data, comprise: (1) Copy number, assigned by the issuing headquarters to each copy (not shown on attached annexes; a log is kept of copies issued to addressees); (2) the official designation of the command, always capitalized, using a code name if required for security; (3) the place of issue, which may be a code name, postal designator, or geographic location/coordinates, always capitalized; (4) the date or date-time group the plan/order is signed, issued, and becomes effective unless otherwise specified; and (5) the message reference number, assigned by the originator (letters, numbers, or both), unconnected to the message center numbering system - annexes issued separately receive different reference numbers to allow acknowledgment in the clear. Figure J-1 illustrates lines 1-15.

Line 8, Title: orders are numbered consecutively for the calendar year; two or more orders issued the same day receive consecutive numbers. A joint operation plan or order is so designated, and any code name is shown.
Line 9 is the Type of Document.

Lines 10-13, References, always appear (use 'References: None' when applicable) and list documents such as maps, charts, photo maps, or standing operating procedures necessary for recipients to understand the order; map entries include series number, country, sheet names/numbers, edition, and scale.

Line 14, Time Zone, may be omitted if the time zone is the same at the place of issue and execution and remains constant throughout execution; if the area of execution has a different time zone, as often occurs in amphibious or airborne operations, this entry states when the indicated time zone becomes effective.

Line 15, Task Organization, may be shown: as an unnumbered entry before paragraph 1 (Situation) when the entire issuing command is organized into task organizations too complex for other methods; as 'No change' if there is no change from the previous task organization; under the appropriate subparagraph of paragraph 3 (the simplest and preferred method in a continuing ground combat situation, e.g., 'No change except paragraph 3b...'); or as an annex when lengthy (e.g., for a division or higher), which is used in amphibious operations because it permits early dissemination and assists concurrent planning, and where planning precedes the operation by a considerable period of time. The first entry is the organization of the issuing headquarters (including Service/administrative groupings performing normal functions); each subsequent task grouping receiving a tactical mission is shown in the sequence the missions are assigned in paragraph 3. Figure J-1 illustrates lines 1-15 in a sample format.

Lines 17-18, General: for plans, this describes the general politico-military environment establishing the probable preconditions for execution; for orders, it can be the commander's estimate of the situation. Both include information obtained during the ongoing design effort.
Line 19, Battlespace, includes the higher commander's area of operation and the command's areas of interest, influence, and operations, described by physical area and forces of concern.

Line 20, Enemy Forces, includes information vital to the entire command or likely to affect mission accomplishment; it may refer to the intelligence annex, operation overlay, or intelligence summaries, and contains disposition, intent, objectives, vulnerabilities, centers of gravity, and courses of action.

Line 21, Friendly Forces, includes information on own forces (higher, adjacent, supporting) bearing on the operation. Artillery is listed as the first supporting unit, then others alphabetically; this line may reference an annex or the operation overlay.
Line 22, Attachments and Detachments, covers nonorganic units attached to and/or organic units temporarily detached from the unit.
Lines 23-25, Paragraph 2 (Mission), is the mission statement, which has no subparagraphs and is always stated here even if also shown on an operation overlay or map.
Line 26, Paragraph 3, addresses Execution.

Line 27, Commander's Intent, is the commander's personal, clearly and concisely written expression of the operation's purpose and the desired end state; its purpose is to allow subordinates to exercise judgment and initiative - to depart from the plan when an assigned task is no longer appropriate to the situation - in a way consistent with the higher commander's aims.

Line 28, Concept of Operations, is a summary statement of how the operation will be accomplished, amplifying paragraph 2 by providing method, end state, and other considerations; it may be shown graphically or published as an appendix to Annex C, and specific unit designations are not used.

Lines 29-35, Tasks, identify tasks to subordinate elements. The highest-priority task(s) include the purpose ('in order to...'); additional tasks may simply be listed if the purpose is understood. Each organic, attached, or supporting unit/tactical grouping executing a tactical task gets a separate numbered subparagraph, and all tactical tasks must be listed in the body of the basic order. Major subordinate elements are listed: for an offensive order, ground combat units (infantry first, then artillery and combat support numerically/alphabetically), aviation combat units or elements (aircraft units, combat support, combat service support), then combat service support units or logistic elements; for a defensive order, units closest to the enemy first, then other ground/aviation combat units in the forward defense area numerically, then remaining units alphabetically. Each tactical task assignment may first show available assets (attached or in support), then enumerate tasks in priority or sequential order.
Line 36, Reserve, is tasked separately from the remainder of the units and is usually designated the main effort when committed; if no reserve is designated, that is so stated.

Line 37, Commander's Critical Information Requirements (CCIRs), identifies information the commander deems critical for maintaining situational awareness, planning future activities, and assisting timely, informed decision-making. CCIRs consist of numbered priority intelligence requirements (PIRs) and friendly force information requirements (e.g., 'PIR #1: Is the 2d Centralian Armored Brigade crossing the Green River?'), each including anticipated decisions and associated branches and sequels developed during the Marine Corps Planning Process. Operations divided into multiple phases may have separate CCIR lists per phase.

Line 38, Coordinating Instructions, is the final subparagraph of paragraph 3, containing instructions common to two or more units, coordinating details and control measures applicable to the command as a whole, and the time or conditions for plan execution; it refers to annexes or references for coordinating details as appropriate. Communications instructions are shown only in paragraph 5.

Line 39, Paragraph 4, contains logistic and personnel information and instructions for the operation; at minimum it summarizes the concept of logistics and directs readers to the appropriate annexes and appendices.
Line 40 is the Page number and Line 41 is the Classification, closing page one of the OPLAN/OPORD; Figure J-2 illustrates lines 16-41.
Page two of the OPLAN/OPORD begins again with Line 1, Classification (illustrated in Figure J-3).

Lines 2-6, Paragraph 5 (Command and Signal), establish and maintain command and signal procedures, covering: Command Relationships (used in a large operation or when relationships are unusual, otherwise omitted; not restated here if already clarified in the task organization); Command Posts and Headquarters (may reference the operations overlay for locations); Succession to Command (designates command succession for the operation); and Signal, which usually references Annex K and other communications publications (e.g., standing operating procedures or communications-electronics operating instructions) and includes instructions or restrictions such as radio restrictions or pyrotechnic signals. Additional subparagraphs may show the location/time of opening communications centers, recognition and identification instructions, code words and names, and liaisons.
Line 7, Acknowledgment Instructions, is included in every order and in separately issued portions, ensuring recipients receive and understand the order.

Lines 8-10, Signature and Authentication: the basic operation plan or order and each annex within are signed or authenticated by the commander using full signature blocks; appropriate officers may be given authority to sign portions, though the commander alone is authorized to sign or approve any portion unless by-direction authority has been granted. Appendices, tabs, exhibits, and maps do not require signature or authentication except when distributed separately from the basic order/plan. The original is signed by the commander with name, rank and service, and title.

Lines 11-34, Annexes, form a portion of the completed plan or order, pertaining to a particular concept, subject, or coordination aspect too voluminous, of insufficient general interest, or in an irregular form (overlays, graphs, tables) for the body of the plan/order; they amplify and clarify the basic plan/order and are themselves amplified by appendices, tabs to appendices, and exhibits to tabs as needed. Annex sequence and lettering must not be changed, though annexes may be omitted when not required (noted 'not used'/'not applicable' in the table of contents, or 'to be issued' if developed later); annex formats/designations in this appendix are mandatory unless otherwise indicated, with the annex title in upper/lower case (also parenthesized within the basic plan/order body). Annex format is preferred for other attachments, such as appendices or tabs, but may be altered when including information or instructions for which no provision is made in the standard format. Additional annexes may be added when necessary for separate distribution or for information with no provision in the standard format. Usually Annexes A, B, C, D, J, and K are provided as part of the basic order/plan; additional annexes and appendices should be developed in abbreviated format for areas significantly affecting mission accomplishment.

Lines 35-39, Authentication, appear on all copies other than the original when the commander's or executive officer's signature is on the original only; authentication is by the deputy, executive officer, chief of staff, or G-3/S-3, and the original is signed by the chief of staff/executive officer as 'OFFICIAL' with name, rank and service, and title.
Line 40 is the Page number and Line 41 the Classification, closing page two of the sample format (Figure J-3).

Section II provides examples of a plan summary, basic operation plan or order, and select annexes, appendices, and tabs. Sample formats are descriptive, identifying information needed for the appropriate paragraph; commanders may modify the format for annexes and appendices, including using graphs and slides, to meet unit and operational needs. The appendix's own table of contents lists all standing formats (only a subset, shown in bold in the source, is reproduced in full in this section); examples for many annexes and appendices not reproduced here may be found in CJCSM 3130.03B, Planning and Execution Formats and Guidance. That Marine Corps-specific table of contents (a five-page nested listing of annexes with their appendices, tabs, and exhibits, condensed here to its annex level) catalogs: Plan Summary; Basic Order or Plan; Annex A (Task Organization); Annex B (Intelligence); Annex C (Operations); Annex D (Logistics/Combat Service Support); Annex E (Personnel); Annex G (Civil-Military Operations); Annex H (Meteorological and Oceanographic Operations); Annex I (Information); Annex J (Command Relationships); Annex K (Combat Information Systems); Annex L (Environmental Considerations); Annex M (Geospatial Information and Services); Annex N (Space Operations); Annex P (Host-Nation Support); Annex Q (Medical Services); Annex R (Reports); Annex S (Special Technical Operations); Annex T (Network Engagement); Annex U (Information Management); Annex V (Interagency/Interorganizational Coordination); Annex W (Aviation Operations); Annex X (Execution Checklist); and Annex Z (Distribution) - no Annex F, O, or Y appears in the Marine Corps-specific list.

subsections.subheader: Sample Format of a Plan Summary

paragraphs.details: A plan summary allows commanders, staffs, and other individuals and agencies to quickly review a command's envisioned activities; it is particularly useful for creating situational awareness in newly assigned personnel and in higher, supporting, and adjacent commands, and is normally prepared only at higher levels of command (e.g., Marine Corps component commands and Marine expeditionary force) in support of a unified command plan.

Paragraph 1 (Purpose) describes the purpose to be achieved by executing the plan and the desired end state (and, if a supporting plan, what plan it supports), including a statement that the summary is based on planning factors and estimates available at preparation time and must be updated before use.

Paragraph 2 (Conditions for Implementation/Execution) summarizes the politico-military situation under which the plan's execution should be considered and any legal considerations affecting implementation (status of forces, rules of engagement, international agreements, law of armed conflict).

Paragraph 3 (Operations to be Conducted) summarizes forces assigned/attached/supporting and required augmentation; deployment movements and any operational security measures; the general nature of combat operations (which may be discussed by phase, including a mission statement, commander's intent, and concept of operations for each phase, end states, and estimated enemy intent); required supporting plans; and collateral plans that could be implemented before, during, or after the subject plan.

Paragraph 4 (Key Assumptions) lists assumptions essential to the plan's success, including degree of mobilization and mobility (sealift/airlift) assumed. Paragraph 5 (Operational Constraints) lists major factors that may impede mission accomplishment.

Paragraph 6 (Time to Commence Effective Operations) may include a table of the required time-phased buildup of combat forces in the objective area, indicating which forces must be available before effective operations can begin and the elapsed time for each significant force level up to the plan's maximum, with any table assumptions noted. Forces are considered at normal readiness conditions (no preparations except force protection). Additional factors to consider, as appropriate, include: time for information-operations preparations and for order preparation/transmission; reaction time including movement preparations and staging; availability/capability of strategic transportation resources; time en route considering lift and route restrictions; possible enemy action against forces in transit; reception/throughput capability of overseas terminals; time to marry up forces and equipment (including prepositioned equipment); availability/capability of in-theater transport systems; and time in the operational area for final force preparation before employment.

Paragraph 7 (Command Relationships) summarizes the command arrangements on execution. Paragraph 8 (Logistic Appraisal) and Paragraph 9 (Personnel Appraisal) provide estimates of logistic and personnel feasibility for the plan.

Paragraph 10 (Consolidated Listing and Impact Assessment of Shortfalls and Limiting Factors) provides a consolidated listing and impact assessment of force, movement, and support shortfalls, including shortfalls in joint/Service doctrine, interoperability, and training, and the tasks that cannot be accomplished due to shortfalls; documentation of each shortfall and mitigation efforts belongs in the appropriate plan annex. It also addresses additional recommended-but-not-allocated forces, which are not to be included in Appendix 2 to Annex A (Task Organization).

subsections.subheader: Sample Format of a Basic Order or Plan

paragraphs.details: The basic order/plan sample format follows the heading data, references, time zone, and task organization entries described in Section I, then Paragraph 1 (Situation) with subparagraphs for General (probable preconditions, US policy goals, and the commander's design/understanding of the operational environment - may be omitted); Battlespace (Joint Operations Area/Higher Commander's Area of Operations, Area of Interest, and Area of Operations, each may include a map); Enemy Forces (location, disposition, capabilities, possible actions, centers of gravity, referencing Annex B); Friendly Forces (higher/adjacent/supporting forces and their missions/relationships, friendly centers of gravity, and tasks of associated government/international/nongovernment/host-nation organizations); Civilian Populace (tribal, religious, or ethnic factors affecting operations); Attachments and Detachments; Assumptions (omitted in orders); and Legal Considerations.

Paragraph 2 (Mission) is a concise who/what/when/where/why/how statement. Paragraph 3 (Execution) contains Commander's Intent (purpose and, optionally, desired end state, to enable subordinate initiative); Concept of Operations (a written and graphic statement of what/how, providing a basis for supporting concepts of maneuver, fires, support, and other concepts per the appropriate annex); Tasks (numbered subparagraphs per subordinate commander, in priority/sequence, with main/supporting effort designated, following the same offensive/defensive unit-listing sequence used elsewhere in this appendix); Reserve (tasks and planning priorities for the reserve force); Commander's Critical Information Requirements (as described in Section I, with the added note that they help the commander tailor the command and control organization and are central to effective information management, which directs the processing, flow, and use of information throughout the force); and Coordinating Instructions (instructions applicable to the entire command or to two or more of its elements that are necessary for proper coordination but not appropriate for a particular annex, establishing the conditions for execution and providing information about the timing of execution and deployments). The commander assigns subordinate commanders the tasks deemed necessary to fulfill the concept of operations, and the synchronization matrix is the chief resource for assigning tasks to subordinates.

Paragraph 4 (Administration and Logistics) covers Personnel (referring to Annex E: personnel facilities, accountability/strength reporting, staffing, reconstitution, rotation policies, individual augmentation); Logistics (referring to Annex D: sustainment priorities, base development, civil engineering, host-nation support, inter-Service responsibilities, movement priorities, ports, transportation policy, logistics assumptions); Communication Strategy and Operations (or refer to Annex I, Appendix 4); Civil-Military Operations (or refer to Annex G); Meteorological and Oceanographic Services (or refer to Annex H); Geospatial Information and Services (or refer to Annex M); and Medical Services (referring to Annex Q for hospitalization/evacuation planning and Annex P for host-nation medical support).

Paragraph 5 (Command and Signal) covers Command Relationships (or refer to Annex J, including changes to major commands and memoranda of understanding); Command Posts and Headquarters (designations/locations of echelons, including displacement timing); Succession to Command; and Signal (or refer to Annex K, including communications-electronics restrictions and system/procedure emphasis). The sample closes with acknowledgment-receipt and signature blocks and an explicit ANNEXES list: A-Task Organization, B-Intelligence, C-Operations, D-Logistics/Combat Service Support, E-Personnel, G-Civil-Military Operations, H-Meteorological and Oceanographic Operations, I-Information, J-Command Relationships, K-Combat Information Systems, L-Environmental Considerations, M-Geospatial Information and Services, N-Space Operations, P-Host-Nation Support, Q-Medical Services, R-Reports, S-Special Technical Operations, T-Network Engagement, U-Information Management, V-Interagency/Interorganizational Coordination, W-Aviation Operations, X-Execution Checklist, and Z-Distribution (F, O, and Y are not used).

subsections.subheader: Sample Format of Annex A (Task Organization)

paragraphs.details: Task organization is the commander's plan for grouping organic and attached combat, combat support, and combat service support units to employ forces in support of the scheme of maneuver. Simple groupings may be shown in paragraph 3 of the basic OPORD/OPLAN; complex groupings are shown in a separate appendix or just before paragraph 1. At minimum, the task organization lists all major commands/task groupings directly subordinate to the issuing commander and all directly supporting organizations (designated 'support' though not under the supported commander's command); organizations established specifically to implement the order/plan also appear. Level of detail should convey only a clear understanding of significant committed forces; commands may use a graphic (e.g., wire diagram) or written format.

In written task organizations, underlining indicates an assigned task; successive subordinate echelons are shown by indentation beneath the underlined unit. Units with no assigned task and not included in another grouping are indented and listed immediately after the issuing headquarters. Subordinate units/groupings with assigned tasks are underlined and sequenced by unit type and mission type: for offensive operations, ground combat units/elements first (infantry, then artillery/combat support numerically or alphabetically), then aviation combat units/elements, then combat service support/logistic elements; for defensive operations, units closest to the enemy first, then remaining ground/aviation combat units in the forward defense area numerically, then others alphabetically. When the Marine Corps component commander prepares a supporting plan, Appendix 1 (Time-Phased Force and Deployment List) must be included.

The sample format's body shows the Organization section listing the issuing headquarters first, then subordinate units/task groupings with no assigned task (indented under the issuing headquarters), then subordinate units/task groupings with assigned tasks, then organic/attached units indented under those, then units providing support (with the type of support - general or direct - shown in parentheses), and finally the reserve unit/task grouping listed last (also shown in its normal sequence if it will be reserve only in the future). The annex lists three appendices (1-Time-Phased Force and Deployment List, 2-Shortfall Identification, 3-Flexible Response and Flexible Deterrent Options) and includes a task organization graphic example depicting a notional MEF wire diagram with subordinate divisions, wings, logistics groups, and reserve, and a block for naming the commanders of the parent organization and principal units.

Annex B (Intelligence) provides detailed information/intelligence on the enemy/adversary and the battlespace and guidance on intelligence and counterintelligence functions. The G-2/S-2 prepares it based on the completed intelligence estimate, providing encyclopedic and current data on the enemy/adversary (order of battle, commander biographical data, capabilities, intentions, and especially the most likely and most dangerous courses of action) and battlespace information (climate, topography, geography, terrain, infrastructure, cultural and political factors), which may reference prior intelligence estimates/reports to reduce annex length. It normally provides intelligence preparation of the battlespace products (e.g., situation template, modified combined obstacle overlay), typically found in Appendix 11 (Intelligence Estimate) or Appendix 12 (Intelligence Products).

Paragraph 1 (Situation) covers Characteristics of the Area (physical, economic, political, medical, social, religious, psychological conditions, without repeating the basic order's general situation); Hydrographic, Amphibious, Topographic, and Weather factors (referring to Annex H and Annex M for hydrographic/amphibious, topographic - trafficability, key terrain, obstacles, cover, concealment, avenues of approach - and climate/weather data); and Estimate of Enemy/Adversary Capabilities (order of battle, strengths/weaknesses, most likely and most dangerous courses of action, and the enemy's own intelligence collection/dissemination capability, with intelligence cutoff dates noted).

Paragraph 2 (Mission and Concept of Intelligence Operations) states the command's mission and outlines the purpose of intelligence operations, summarizing the means and agencies used to plan, direct, collect, process, exploit, produce, disseminate, and evaluate intelligence, integrating other Services'/allied resources when appropriate.

Paragraph 3 (Intelligence Activities) identifies intelligence resources and required planning/direction/collection/processing/production/dissemination/evaluation efforts, proceeding from priority intelligence requirements through capabilities/resources planning to intelligence-element tasking: Planning and Direction (determining requirements, preparing a collection plan, issuing collection orders/requests, monitoring collection agencies, noting exceptions to standard procedures, and identifying PIRs - placed in Appendix 1 if lengthy - and new intelligence requirements); Processing and Exploitation (converting information into usable form, including translation and imagery/signals/technical sensor processing); Production (analyzing/reporting collected intelligence, multidiscipline fused reporting, production of intelligence/counterintelligence products); and Dissemination (procedures for vertical/lateral dissemination, alternate means during crises, required reports and formats, distribution of studies, releasability to allied nations, and secondary imagery dissemination).

Paragraph 4 (Assignment of Intelligence Tasks) provides Orders to Subordinate and Attached Units and Requests to Higher, Adjacent, and Cooperating Units (each in separate numbered subparagraphs, including allied/coalition forces) and Coordinating Instructions (periodic/special intelligence-officer conferences and intelligence liaison arrangements). Paragraph 5 (Communications System) summarizes US and non-US communications supporting the intelligence function or references Annex K, including interoperability comments. Paragraph 6 (Miscellaneous Instructions) covers items such as operations security, deception, disclosure of intelligence, releasability to coalition forces, communication strategy and operations, specialized intelligence personnel/augmentation, and exploitation of captured materiel/documents. The annex lists 17 appendices covering PIRs, signals intelligence, counterintelligence, targeting intelligence, human intelligence, intelligence support to operations in the information environment, imagery intelligence, measurement and signature intelligence, captured enemy equipment, national intelligence support team, intelligence estimate, intelligence products, intelligence collection plan, reconnaissance and surveillance plan, geographic intelligence, intelligence operations, and support to survival/evasion/resistance/escape.

Annex C (Operations) provides substantive guidance for conducting operations, amplifying (not simply repeating) the basic OPORD's information and concepts; plans for employing non-US forces should include proposed command arrangements and consideration of essential combat/logistic support requirements. Paragraph 1 (General) states the annex's purpose, restates the mission and area of operations (including any reconnaissance/surveillance authorizations), and refers to the basic order/plan for the situation. Paragraph 2 (Concept of Operations) is placed here, rather than in the basic order/plan, when lengthy and detailed, and refers to Appendix 16 (Operations Overlay). Paragraph 3 (Conduct of Operations) provides guidance not already in the basic OPORD and overviews included Annex C appendices/tabs. Paragraph 4 (Operational Constraints) lists constraints not enumerated elsewhere (e.g., deployment/employment impacts on airfield ramp space, host-nation support), estimates their impact, and states how the concept of operations/tasks would change if constraints were removed or incrementally lifted. Paragraph 5 (Command and Signal) refers to the basic order/plan (Command) and to the basic order/plan or Annex K (Signal). The annex lists 24 appendices spanning nuclear operations, CBRN defense, special operations, evasion/recovery, risk, rules of engagement, reconnaissance, air base operability, noncombatant evacuation, explosive ordnance disposal, amphibious operations, force protection, rear area operations, cyberspace operations, liaison plan, operations overlay, fire support, countermechanized plan, obstacle and barrier plan, breaching plan, decision support matrix/template, operation assessment plan, enemy prisoners of war/civilian internees plan, and authorities matrix.

subsections.subheader: Sample Format of Appendix 16 (Operations Overlay) to Annex C

paragraphs.details: Appendix 16 (Operations Overlay) uses appropriate marks and graphics from MIL-STD-2525D, Department of Defense Interface Standard: Joint Military Symbology, to visually depict the operation; an operation divided into phases/stages may require multiple overlays. The overlay is based on the approved course of action graphic, must clearly depict the concept of operations, and should balance necessary detail against simplicity (an overly dense, cluttered overlay is counterproductive). It may depict: form of maneuver; main and supporting effort purposes/tasks; reserve location and priorities; control measures (fire support coordination measures, maneuver control measures, airspace coordination measures); boundaries; objectives; command posts; rear area boundaries and associated units; named and target areas of interest; combat service support areas; airfields; beaches; ports; forward arming and refueling points; ISR locations; enemy/adversary and adjacent forces; civilian groups; routes and axes; obstacles; essential fire support tasks; and operations-in-the-information-environment support tasks.

subsections.subheader: Sample Format of Annex D (Logistics/Combat Service Support)

paragraphs.details: Logistics is the science of planning and carrying out the movement and maintenance of forces, including combat service support at the tactical level and movement/sustainment of Marine forces at the operational level; it provides the commander the means to conduct and win battles, campaigns, and the war. Annex D (Logistics/Combat Service Support) directs and guides subordinate commanders and staffs on logistics/CSS provision in support of the OPORD/OPLAN (the theory and philosophy are in MCDP 4, Logistics; detailed combat-service-support and planning-document guidance is in MCTP 3-40.B, Tactical-Level Logistics). Annex D addresses command and control of logistic/CSS organizations (including relationships and C2 support requirements), is integrated with maneuver, fires, and force protection concepts, and needs only the depth necessary for subordinate understanding; the G-4/S-4 normally prepares it with logistic combat element involvement, reflecting phasing and anticipated mission/task changes, with detailed/specialized information placed in subparagraphs or appendices. Aviation-specific logistic functions, such as supply and maintenance, are discussed in or referred to Appendix 1 or the aviation combat element's own OPORD/OPLAN (the source labels that cross-reference 'Appendix 1 (Supply)' although Appendix 1 of this annex is Petroleum, Oils, and Lubricants Supply and Appendix 7 is Supply - a source-level inconsistency, preserved).

Paragraph 1 (Situation) covers Enemy (referring to Annex B: enemy actions/intent to disrupt friendly logistics/CSS, and enemy capabilities/assets that could augment friendly operations); Friendly (supporting logistic/CSS organizations not subordinate to the force and their assigned missions); Infrastructure (referring to Annex B: ports, factories, fuel/water sources, lines of communications usable for friendly logistics/CSS); Attachments and Detachments (referring to Annex A: logistic/CSS units attached from other Services/nations, and Marine Corps logistic/CSS units detached to support other forces); Assumptions (omitted in orders); Resource Availability (competing demands where requirements may exceed resources, with recommended solutions and assured host-nation support); and Planning Factors (use of approved planning factors/formulas except where experience/local conditions dictate otherwise, with deviations identified and justified).

Paragraph 2 (Mission) restates the command's mission from the base order. Paragraph 3 (Execution) states the Concept of Logistics and Combat Service Support (how logistic/CSS assets will be organized and positioned, including other-Service/nation forces, host-nation support, and lines-of-communications operation) and assigns Tasks: logistic/CSS responsibilities to subordinate logistic organizations; responsibility for logistics/CSS required from other commands, Services, or nations; responsibility for logistics/CSS required for forces assigned/attached from other commands, Services, or nations; responsibility for logistics/CSS required for Marine Corps forces assigned/attached elsewhere; and responsibilities supporting joint boards/committees (e.g., transportation, procurement) and other Services/nations providing services.

Paragraph 4 (Administration and Logistics), subparagraph a (Logistics and Combat Service Support), begins with Supply (referring to Appendix 7), summarizing, if different from standard planning factors: Distribution and Allocation (purpose/location/projected displacement of supply depots, terminals, and ports; prepositioned logistic resource allocation; existing terminal/lines-of-communications throughput capability and time-phased expansion needed); Level of Supply (time-phased operating/safety levels; prepositioned war reserve materiel requirements; special materiel-support arrangements; anticipated shortfalls; common-user logistic supply support arrangements); Salvage (collection/classification/disposition instructions and logistic impact); Captured Enemy/Adversary Materiel (collection/classification/disposition instructions, referring to Annex B and to Appendix 10 to Annex B for captured cryptographic equipment); and Local Acquisition of Supplies and Services (see Joint Publication 4-01, The Defense Transportation System, and the current version of DoD Instruction 1100.22, Policy and Procedures for Determining Workforce Mix; categories of available/emergency-source goods and services, dependability of local acquisition/labor sources, and a statement that essential contractor services have been reviewed for OPLAN-execution essentiality and continuity).

Supply concludes with Petroleum, Oils, and Lubricants (referring to Appendix 1). The remainder of subparagraph a covers External Support (referring to Appendix 11: type/quantity of support, inter-Service/cross-Service arrangements, current or planned support arrangements, and foreign/host-nation support) and Maintenance (referring to Appendix 12: maintenance-facility requirements and the level/location of maintenance to be performed, including host-nation or contractor facilities).

Subparagraph a continues with Transportation (referring to Appendix 4: general planning/execution guidance including movement and use priorities, and a Mobility Support Force and Movement Feasibility Analysis addressing lift resources, airfield/seaport/aerial-port capabilities, throughput capability, and adverse movement factors such as ramp-space impacts and host-nation support); General Engineering Support Plan (referring to Appendix 13, stating rationale if Appendix 5, Civil Engineering Support Plan, is not prepared); Health Services (referring to Appendix 9); Services (referring to Appendix 8); Mortuary Affairs (referring to Appendix 2, or otherwise stating applicable activities/policy); Ammunition (referring to Appendix 6, Nonnuclear Ammunition, or discussing critical ammunition issues affecting mission accomplishment); Aviation Logistic Support (referring to Appendix 10 or the aviation combat element's own Annex D); and Operational Security Planning Guidance for Logistics (referring to Appendix 11 to Annex I: comprehensive OPSEC guidance addressing base, facility, installation, stock, physical, and lines-of-communications security to promote essential secrecy).

Subparagraph b (Administration) provides general administrative guidance for logistic/CSS operations, including report formats, timing, methods, and classification of submission. Paragraph 5 (Command and Signal) covers Command Relationships (referring to Annex J for relationships external to logistic units and providing support relationships) and Communications System (referring to Annex K for detailed requirements, with a general statement of scope/type of communications required). The annex lists 13 appendices: Petroleum/Oils/Lubricants Supply, Mortuary Affairs, Sustainability Analysis, Mobility and Transportation, Civil Engineering Support Plan, Nonnuclear Ammunition, Supply, Services, Health Services, Aviation Logistic Support, External Support, Maintenance, and General Engineering.

Operations in the information environment (OIE) are actions taken to generate, preserve, or apply military information power to increase and protect competitive advantage or combat power potential across all domains; military information power is defined as the total means of force or information capability applied against a relevant actor to enhance lethality, survivability, mobility, or influence - exerting will or influence through the generation, preservation, denial, or projection of information. Annex I (Information) integrates the information warfighting function so that Marine Corps OIE are planned in concert with MAGTF operations across all domains, persistently across the competition continuum and armed conflict, in support of naval, Service, combatant command, and joint force objectives. OIE are planned/executed via seven functions/tasks: assure enterprise C2 and critical systems; provide information environment battlespace awareness; attack and exploit networks, systems, and information; inform domestic and international audiences; influence foreign target audiences; deceive foreign target audiences; and control OIE capabilities, resources, and activities - using six capability areas: electromagnetic spectrum operations, cyberspace operations, space operations, influence operations, deception operations, and inform operations. OIE occur across the full range of military operations; MAGTF information plans must nest within the joint force commander's plan and require whole-of-staff coordination, with intelligence support being critical.

The annex should clearly state the primary tasks of each applicable OIE function/task, identifying how a specific capability within a capability area accomplishes the task (and how capabilities from other warfighting functions, e.g., fires and maneuver, may support it - for example, the 'Assure Command and Control' task may require physical attack of enemy long-range precision fires targeting friendly C2 nodes, plus defensive cyberspace operations, electronic attack, and electronic warfare support), providing enough guidance to synchronize these elements and detailed execution instructions in subsequent tabs. Paragraph 1 (Situation) covers Enemy/Adversary (situation, disposition, intelligence capabilities, courses of action bearing on planned OIE); Friendly (friendly-force situation affecting information objectives, critical limitations, and other planned OIE); and Assumptions (omitted in orders).

Paragraph 2 (Mission) restates the command's mission from the basic OPORD. Paragraph 3 (Execution) covers Concept of Support (how the commander visualizes OIE execution from beginning to termination, integration of information tasks into the CONOPS, and supervision/termination concepts, potentially divided by phase); OIE Tasks, identifying major tasks for each of the seven functions/tasks not already captured elsewhere in the order (assure enterprise C2/critical systems; provide information environment battlespace awareness; attack/exploit networks/systems/information; inform domestic/international audiences; influence foreign target audiences; deceive foreign target audiences; control OIE capabilities/resources/activities; electromagnetic spectrum operations; cyberspace operations; civil-military operations; operations security; and signature management); and Coordinating Instructions addressing mutual support among OIE elements.

Paragraph 4 (Administration and Logistics) addresses OIE administrative/logistic requirements. Paragraph 5 (Command and Control) lists OIE command-and-control instructions, states the OIE command structure, and identifies special OIE communications/reporting requirements. The annex lists 11 appendices covering assure enterprise C2 and critical systems; provide information environment battlespace awareness; attack and exploit networks/systems/information; inform domestic and international audiences; influence foreign target audiences; deceive foreign target audiences; control OIE capabilities/resources/activities; electromagnetic spectrum operations; cyberspace operations; civil-military operations; and operations security.

subsections.subheader: Sample Format for Tab A (Military Deception) to Appendix 6 to Annex I

paragraphs.details: Tab A (Military Deception) provides background and guidance for preparing the military deception tab of joint plans and orders; the process for joint military deception planning is established in JP 3-13.4, Military Deception. As general policy, all material related to planned, ongoing, or completed military deception is accorded controlled access on a need-to-know basis (limited to those planning, approving, or executing the deception). The deception tab is normally developed, published, distributed, and maintained separately from the rest of the OPLAN, using only positive-control distribution means (e.g., hand-to-hand delivery, secure electronic communications) rather than standard administrative procedures; specific deception events (e.g., unit movements) may appear in the basic OPLAN/annexes if not identified as deception-related, and deception documents carry cover sheets annotated per CJCSI 3211.01, Joint Policy for Military Deception, which also establishes review criteria that deception planners must follow for approval.

Paragraph 1 (Situation) covers General (see basic order/plan); Enemy (General Capabilities relating to the planned deception; Deception Targets - the political/military/economic decision makers targeted, their personalities/strengths/weaknesses/vulnerabilities and influencing factors; Target Biases and Predispositions; and Probable Enemy Course of Action, referring to Annex B); Friendly (situation, critical limitations, concept of operations); and Assumptions. Paragraph 2 (Mission) covers the Operational Mission (extracted from the basic order/plan) and the Deception Mission: Deception Goal (the desired end state, e.g., 'to cause the enemy to weight their defense in the eastern corridor...'), Deception Objective(s) (desired enemy action/inaction), Desired Enemy Perceptions (what the target must believe), and Deception Story (the scenario of friendly actions/capabilities to be portrayed, potentially an alternate course of action to the one actually chosen).

Paragraph 3 (Execution) covers Concept of the Operation: General (framework and phases); Other OIE Elements (use of, and coordination/deconfliction with, other OIE elements); Feedback and Monitoring (expected feedback type/collection method and the impact of its absence); Means (available deception assets); Tasks (execution and feedback taskings); and Risks (rated low/moderate/high, detailed in Exhibit 3 to this tab, covering: deception succeeds - likely enemy response and intelligence-sharing impact; deception fails - impact if the target ignores or fails to act on it; and deception is compromised to allies or enemy/adversaries). Coordinating Instructions address tasks spanning two or more units, tentative D-day/H-hour, and other coordination requirements.

Paragraph 4 (Administration and Logistics) states administrative/logistic support procedures for developing, coordinating, and implementing the deception plan (excluding administrative, logistic, or medical actions that are themselves part of the deception, which are placed in Exhibit 4), covering Administration (general and specific procedures), Logistics (requirements such as transportation of special material or printing equipment/materials, per Exhibit 4), and Costs. Paragraph 5 (Communications System) covers Command Relationships (via Exhibit 5, by phase: Approval authority, Authority designating supported/supporting commanders per Exhibit 1/5, Oversight of nonorganic executions, and Coordination requirements in/out of theater) and Communications (means, procedures, and reporting requirements for control personnel and participants). Paragraph 6 (Security) covers General procedures and Specific access restrictions, handling instructions, authority to grant access, and use of cover stories/code words/nicknames, with access rosters placed in a separate document if required. The tab lists seven exhibits: Task Organization, Intelligence, Operations, Administration and Logistics, Command Relationships, Execution Schedule, and Distribution.

subsections.subheader: Sample Format of Exhibit 2 (Intelligence) to Tab A to Appendix 6 to Annex I

paragraphs.details: Exhibit 2 (Intelligence) to Tab A provides intelligence focused and specific to the deception, without repeating Annex B (Intelligence). Paragraph 1 (Deception CONOPS) concisely states the executing command, deception target, objective(s), and duration. Paragraph 2 (Situation) covers Enemy/Adversary in depth: Target Description (decision makers/organizations targeted, their personalities/strengths/weaknesses/vulnerabilities); Target Biases and Predispositions; Enemy/Adversary Intelligence Organizations (missions, methods, covert/clandestine capabilities, and which are most likely to inform the target or expose the deception); Enemy/Adversary Counterintelligence Organizations; Enemy/Adversary Intelligence-Sharing with Other Countries; Other Sources and Related Matters (scientific/technical/diplomatic/academic information conduits); Deception and Denial Activities (the target's own use of deception/denial); Target Reaction (estimated reaction if the deception succeeds or fails, and likelihood of countering deception, feeding the risk assessments in Tab A and its Exhibit 3); and Third-Party Reaction (impact on allies, neutrals, and other potential adversaries, also feeding those risk assessments); plus Friendly (activities by unknowing US forces affecting the deception, and a comparison of intelligence collection/processing/reporting timelines against the plan's operational timeline).

Paragraph 3 (Intelligence Requirements) covers Priority Intelligence Requirements (listed in Attachment A); Feedback (an assessment of the intelligence community's ability to collect plan-specific feedback); and Assignment of Intelligence Tasks (identifying Service intelligence agencies/organizations, the commander's own intelligence organizations/assets, and others to produce plan-specific collection requirements). The exhibit lists two attachments: A - Priority Intelligence Requirements, and B - Others as needed.

subsections.subheader: Sample Format of Attachment A (Priority Intelligence Requirements) to Exhibit 2 to Tab A to Appendix 6 to Annex I

paragraphs.details: Attachment A (Priority Intelligence Requirements) identifies requirements, including those of subordinate commanders, for the pre-execution and execution phases of the planned deception: Paragraph 1 (General) states the identification requirement; Paragraph 2 (Before Implementation of the Order or Plan) lists questions needing answers for further planning and the implementation decision; and Paragraph 3 (Upon Implementation of the Order or Plan) lists additional PIRs and other intelligence requirements that become relevant once the plan is implemented, using additional paragraphs as needed to reflect differing requirements across planned phases.

subsections.subheader: Sample Format of Annex J (Command Relationships)

paragraphs.details: Command relationships are the interrelated responsibilities between commanders and the authority of commanders in the chain of command; unity of effort is achieved largely through a flexible range of command relationships. The joint force commander exercises command during joint operations per JP 1 (Doctrine for the Armed Forces of the United States), JP 3-0 (Joint Operations), and MCDP 1-0, which describe possible command relationships among the joint force commander, Marine Corps component commander, MAGTF commander, and subordinate commanders. This annex discusses coordination requirements between forces in the same/adjacent areas (per JP 1 and the common higher-headquarters order/plan); succession-of-command and alternate C2 planning (referring to basic order/plan paragraph 5 or Annex K); DoD Directive 3025.14 (Evacuation of U.S. Citizens and Designated Aliens from Threatened Areas Abroad) responsibilities requiring close diplomatic-military coordination during tension/hostilities; and relationships between the US Information Agency and the Armed Forces in conducting military information support operations.

Paragraph 1 (General) states the Purpose - establishing relationships among combatant commands, international commands/organizations, the country commander of US forces, Service/functional component commanders, major subordinate commanders, coordinating authorities, other subordinate military activities, US diplomatic missions, supporting government departments/agencies, and forces/agencies of other nations - and the Scope of relationships established (by geographic area or by function, and when/under what circumstances they take effect). Paragraph 2 (Command Lines) addresses Service and Functional Components; Other Subordinate Commands (established command lines and conditions for transfer of operational control); Augmentation Forces (purpose, time, duration, and degree of authority/responsibility); and Alternate Procedures (succession of command and alternate C2 location). Paragraph 3 (Support and Coordination Relationships) addresses Supporting Military Forces; Coordinating Authorities (assigned responsibility for coordinating specific functions); Supporting Agencies (e.g., US Information Agency); Inter-Service Support Arrangements (referring to Annex D, subparagraph 2b(7)); and Coordination with Diplomatic Agencies. Paragraph 4 addresses relationships with international/foreign commands and organizations (including guerrilla organizations) and the conditions for their effectiveness, and Paragraph 5 (Planning Relationships) specifies relationships for developing supporting plans, including coordination with other-nation commands and nonmilitary agencies. The annex lists one appendix: 1-Command Relationships Diagram.

subsections.subheader: Sample Format of Appendix 1 (Command Relationships Diagram) to Annex J

paragraphs.details: Appendix 1 (Command Relationships Diagram) graphically portrays the command relationships established in Annex J, showing all specific relationships such as operational control, tactical control, or administrative control.

subsections.subheader: Sample Format of Annex T (Network Engagement)

paragraphs.details: Annex T (Network Engagement) provides detailed information on interactions with friendly, neutral, and threat networks (comprising people, places, and things - potentially multiple of each in the battlespace) to help achieve the commander's objectives, assisting the commander and staff in understanding the operational environment (with intelligence as a critical component for building the necessary products). Network engagement products support targeting and engagement, generating lethal and nonlethal effects against threat networks, and organizing information to generate nonlethal effects exclusively with friendly and neutral networks through partnership, cooperation, and engagement.

Paragraph 1 (Situation) summarizes and categorizes Friendly networks (e.g., allied military forces, host nation government, international organizations), Neutral networks (e.g., local tribes, labor unions, international organizations), and Threat networks (e.g., nation-state military forces, non-state actors, criminal or terrorist groups) in the battlespace. Paragraph 2 (Mission) restates the command's mission from the basic OPORD.

Paragraph 3 (Execution) covers Concept of Support (how network engagement integrates into the operation) and Network Engagement Products, providing guidance for: Critical Variables (key resources/conditions to shape/maintain for the desired end state); Relevant Networks (those requiring consideration for planning/targeting/engagement, tied to the critical variables); Association Matrix (relationships between nodes in each network, from direct contact); Activities Matrix (connections between a key actor and organizations/events/locations/activities); Network Diagram (graphic display of connections between individuals/organizations/activities); Social Network Analysis (quantitative link-degree data via mathematical computation of node relevancy); Network Function Templates (graphic depiction of network structure-to-function association); and Critical Factors Analysis (identifying each relevant network's critical variables, environmental conditions, critical capabilities, requirements, and vulnerabilities).

Paragraph 3 continues with Targeting and Engagement (summarizing network engagement's support to targeting/engagement, referring to Annex B and Annex C) and Operation Assessment (summarizing support to the operation assessment plan, referring to Appendix 22 to Annex C). Paragraph 4 (Administration and Logistics) addresses network-engagement administrative/logistic requirements, and Paragraph 5 (Command and Signal) lists command-and-control instructions, the supporting command structure, and any special communications/software/reporting requirements. The annex lists eight appendices: Critical Variables, Relevant Networks, Association Matrices, Activities Matrices, Network Diagrams, Social Network Analysis, Network Function Templates, and Critical Factors Analysis.

subsections.subheader: Sample Format of Annex V (Interagency/Interorganizational Coordination)

paragraphs.details: Paragraph 1 (Situation), subparagraph a (General), includes: a Statement that the annex is a brief synopsis of the plan's major elements and the coordination/interaction needed between the command and interagency partners during preparation and execution (subject to modification based on actual conditions); Politico-Military Situation (the preconditions for the plan, national security objectives/interests it serves, and interagency capabilities needed to reach normalcy); Policy Coordination (support requirements to initiate interagency planning); and Planning and Execution Coordination (the proposed interagency coordination concept for unity of effort and deconfliction). Subparagraph b (Assumptions) lists key assumptions affecting interagency planning, and subparagraph c (Legal Considerations) lists legal factors affecting interagency participation.

Paragraph 2 (Mission) restates the command's mission from the base order. Paragraph 3 (Execution) covers Concept of Operations (primary objectives and desired effects per phase; the concept for interagency coordination supporting military operations; commander's interorganizational cooperation and desired government/nongovernmental/private-organization participation per phase - broken down into Commander's Intent for each phase, Major Areas of US Government Response, and Level of Integration envisioned as operations transition between phases); Tasks and Milestones (before handoff to civilian authorities); and Coordinating Instructions for other agencies and organizations.

Paragraph 4 (Administration and Logistics) provides the concept for administrative/logistic support to participating agencies and organizations, covering personnel/property accounting, security/force protection, medical care, transportation, supply classes, maintenance support, office equipment/personnel, and communications assets. Paragraph 5 (Command and Control) identifies unique interagency coordination relationships (e.g., a joint interagency coordination group), the proposed organizational relationship/chain of responsibility, and the chain of authority for both US Government agencies and international organizations. Appendices are 'as required,' potentially including detailed information on key interagency, international-organization, and nongovernmental stakeholders (mission, current/planned programs, locations, points of contact, assessments).

subsections.subheader: Sample Format of Annex X (Execution Checklist)

paragraphs.details: Annex X (Execution Checklist) provides a convenient, useful listing of key events and tasks the force must conduct to accomplish the mission, built from the synchronization matrix (the key Marine Corps Planning Process tool used to create it). It allows subordinate, supporting, and adjacent forces to coordinate actions and maintain situational awareness, and serves as a command-and-control/information-management tool for the combat operations center; critical events and tasks are listed in order of envisioned execution. It is generally displayed as a spreadsheet with columns for line number, unit, task, condition, location, communications nets, brevity code, planned date/time, and blank space for recording actual date/time and notes.

The Joint Orders Table of Contents, added by Change 1 and based on CJCSM 3130.03B, is an example of how a joint plan's table of contents, annexes, appendices, tabs, and exhibits should be numbered (page-code format such as B-1-A-1 for Annex B, Appendix 1, Tab A). The specimen is headed 'CJCSM 3130.03B, 14 June 2024 - EXAMPLE TABLE OF CONTENTS (JOINT ORDERS FORMAT)' for a notional HEADQUARTERS, USXYZ COMMAND (USXYZCOM OPLAN XXXX-24) and opens with front matter preceding the annexes: Letter of Transmittal, Security Instructions and Record of Changes, Plan Summary, Classification Guidance, Table of Contents, and Base plan. It catalogs the following full CJCSM annex structure, each further subdivided into appendices, tabs, and exhibits as needed: Annex A (Task Organization); Annex B (Intelligence); Annex C (Operations); Annex D (Logistics); Annex E (Personnel); Annex F (Public Affairs); Annex G (Civil-Military Operations); Annex H (Meteorological and Oceanographic Operations); Annex I (Knowledge, Information, and Data Management); Annex J (Command Relationships); Annex K (Command, Control, Communications, Computer, and Cybersecurity (C4/Cybersecurity) Systems); Annex L (Environmental Considerations); Annex M (Not Used); Annex N (Assessments); Annex O (Foreign Disclosure Guidance); Annex P (Host-Nation Support); Annex Q (Health Services); Annex R (Reports); Annex S (Special Technical Operations); Annex T (Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Response); Annex U (Notional Counterproliferation Decision Guide); Annex V (Interagency-Interorganizational Coordination); Annex W (Operational Contract Support); Annex X (Execution Checklist); Annex Y (Commanders' Communication Strategy); and Annex Z (Distribution).
